1Presentation
Bottom line
  • Clinical atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD), low-density lipoprotein (LDL) 190 mg/dL or more, or diabetes at 40 to 75 identifies a statin-benefit group before calculation.
  • For remaining adults in the board-style Pooled Cohort Equations pathway, use the 10-year risk, risk enhancers and shared discussion. Low high-density lipoprotein (HDL) is a risk marker, not a drug target.
  • Keep the calculator and its thresholds together. Current risk assessmentThe 2026 guideline recommends Predicting Risk of Cardiovascular Disease Events (PREVENT) equations for primary prevention in adults ages 30 to 79 without known atherosclerotic disease. Its risk bands differ: under 3%, 3% to under 5%, 5% to under 10%, and 10% or more. Do not apply the Pooled Cohort cutoffs to a PREVENT result.
Statin-benefit groups
FindingAction
Clinical ASCVD: prior myocardial infarction, ischemic stroke or peripheral artery diseaseUse a high-intensity statin if tolerated; individualize intensity in older adults.
LDL ≥ 190 mg/dLUse a high-intensity statin without a risk calculation. Severe LDL elevation is often familial; evaluate for familial hypercholesterolemia and assess relatives.
Diabetes, age 40 to 75Use at least moderate intensity; the board deck favors high intensity when Pooled Cohort risk is 7.5% or more.

Periodic risk assessment at ages 40 to 75 includes lipid measurement. The Pooled Cohort Equations are not validated under 40. Screening agesThe USPSTF standalone adult lipid-screening recommendation is archived; its statin recommendation is risk-based. The board deck also teaches lipid screening from age 20, repeated every 4 to 6 years when normal. Pediatric universal screening is usually during ages 9 to 11, with a second screen during ages 17 to 21.Older USPSTF wording used men 35 or older, women 45 or older at increased risk, and younger adults with risk factors; the conventional interval was about every 5 years. These are legacy screening statements, not the current statin-benefit algorithm.

5Diagnostic criteria

Pause point. A low HDL value is not an indication for niacin. Treat LDL-related and overall atherosclerotic risk, rather than the HDL number alone.

6Risk
Pooled Cohort risk bands
10-year riskCategoryAction
Under 5%LowEmphasize lifestyle.
5% to under 7.5%BorderlineDiscuss a statin when risk enhancers favor treatment.
7.5% to under 20%IntermediateDiscuss moderate-intensity statin therapy; use CAC selectively if uncertain.
20% or moreHighUse high-intensity statin therapy when tolerated.

Risk enhancers include premature family history, chronic kidney disease, metabolic syndrome, preeclampsia or early menopause, chronic inflammatory disease, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection and South Asian ancestry. Persistently elevated LDL (160 mg/dL or more) or triglycerides (175 mg/dL or more), apolipoprotein B, lipoprotein(a) and high-sensitivity C-reactive protein may also refine risk.

The US Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) recommends a statin at ages 40 to 75 with a cardiovascular risk factor and estimated 10-year risk of at least 10%; offer one selectively at 7.5% to under 10%. Different recommendation frameworksThe USPSTF recommendation and the older Pooled Cohort-based American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association (ACC/AHA) risk discussion are different frameworks. The 2026 PREVENT framework has different risk categories again. Read the calculator and recommendation named in the question.

8Follow-up
Reassessment
SituationDo
After lifestyle or lipid-lowering treatment changesReassess the lipid response, adherence and treatment tolerance.
Myositis or hepatitis while taking a statinStop the statin and evaluate the adverse effect.
Practice
  1. 48-year-old man asks when his cholesterol should be checked has never had a lipid panel no diabetes or vascular disease Does not smoke; no family history of early heart disease BP 122/78 mm Hg · fasting glucose 90 mg/dL → As part of periodic 10-year risk assessment, ages 40 to 75 → lipid measurement is now part of 10-year risk assessment at ages 40 to 75, not a standalone screen
  2. 52-year-old man comes for a checkup no prior heart attack, stroke or peripheral artery disease LDL 210 mg/dL, confirmed on a repeat panel Father had a heart attack at 50 BP 128/80 mm Hg · fasting glucose 92 mg/dL → High-intensity statin without calculating risk → LDL 190 or higher on repeat is severe hypercholesterolemia, often familial: high-intensity statin with no risk calculation; test relatives
  3. 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes comes for a checkup no prior heart attack, stroke or peripheral artery disease LDL 120 mg/dL Takes metformin; does not smoke BP 124/76 mm Hg · hemoglobin A1c 7.1% → Moderate-intensity statin → diabetes at age 40 to 75 is a statin-benefit group: moderate-intensity statin with no risk calculation
  4. 60-year-old man is seen 3 months after a heart attack treated with a coronary stent LDL 118 mg/dL Takes aspirin and a beta-blocker; not on a statin BP 126/78 mm Hg · HR 64/min → High-intensity statin → a prior myocardial infarction is clinical ASCVD, a statin-benefit group: high-intensity statin with no risk calculation
  5. 34-year-old man asks for his 10-year heart attack and stroke risk smokes 1 pack of cigarettes per day LDL 150 mg/dL No diabetes; no family history of early heart disease BP 124/78 mm Hg · fasting glucose 88 mg/dL → Lifestyle therapy; defer the calculator → he is in no statin-benefit group (no ASCVD, LDL under 190, no diabetes), and the Pooled Cohort Equations are not validated under age 40, so there is no valid risk to calculate; for this smoker, lifestyle therapy means smoking cessation first
  6. 55-year-old man comes to discuss his cholesterol results 10-year risk by the Pooled Cohort Equations is 9% HDL 32 mg/dL; LDL 140 mg/dL No diabetes or known vascular disease BP 134/84 mm Hg · nonsmoker → Moderate-intensity statin after a risk discussion → 7.5% to under 20% is intermediate risk, a moderate-intensity statin; the low HDL is a risk marker, not a drug target
  7. 50-year-old woman comes to review her cholesterol results 10-year risk by the Pooled Cohort Equations is 6% had preeclampsia in both pregnancies Her parents emigrated from India BP 128/78 mm Hg · LDL 165 mg/dL → Start a statin → borderline risk (5% to under 7.5%) with risk enhancers (preeclampsia, South Asian ancestry, LDL 160 or higher) is pushed toward a moderate-intensity statin after a risk discussion
  8. 56-year-old man is undecided about starting a statin 10-year risk by the Pooled Cohort Equations is 8% coronary artery calcium score of 0 No diabetes; never smoked; no early family heart disease BP 130/80 mm Hg · LDL 150 mg/dL → Withhold the statin for now → at uncertain intermediate risk, a calcium score of 0 means a statin may be withheld or delayed unless the patient smokes, has diabetes or has a strong family history of premature ASCVD
  9. 45-year-old woman comes for cardiovascular risk assessment nonfasting sample: triglycerides 520 mg/dL calculated LDL 150 mg/dL She ate breakfast 1 hour before the blood draw BP 128/80 mm Hg · no diabetes → Repeat lipid panel after fasting → triglycerides over 400 on a nonfasting sample make the calculated LDL unreliable: repeat the panel fasting
  10. 55-year-old man asks for a medication to raise his HDL HDL 30 mg/dL; LDL 96 mg/dL 10-year risk by the Pooled Cohort Equations is 4% Exercises daily; does not smoke BP 122/76 mm Hg → No pharmacotherapy → A low HDL value alone does not justify an HDL-raising drug. Extended-release niacin and a CETP inhibitor are not indicated solely for this HDL value; base treatment on LDL and overall atherosclerotic risk.
